messages.subject: IV/IS specifications
messages.body_plain:
Dear GGIR developer,

I have a couple of questions on some of the parameters that can be specified in the GGIR package. I'm working with the UK Biobank data, and since the GGIR package was developed on this data, I was wondering if there was a standard/what the settings are for the following IV/IS parameters:
- IVIS_windowsize_minutes
- IVIS_epochsize_seconds

Additionally, I was wondering how the setting of these parameters interferes with the ws2 epoch size specification.
The vignette is very helpful, but not elaborate enough for me to figure out these parameters and the way they interact.

Many thanks!

Kind regards,
Renske

messages.subject: Re: [GGIR] IV/IS specifications
messages.body_plain:
Dear Renske,

Thanks for researching out.

On side note - About GGIR and UK Biobank, it is more the other way around. UK Biobank gained a lot from the work I did around GGIR. I developed most of GGIR between 2008-2013 using the Whitehall II study and the Pelotas birth cohorts as primary testing ground. My PhD in those years was focussed on guide UK Biobank in deciding whether to use wrist worn accelerometer and how to analyse it. The 2011 PLoSONE study I led on was one of the key reasons for UK Biobank to go ahead with using wrist accelerometry. The algorithms I developed in those years where then later copied to Java software by Doherty and colleagues in their 2017 UK Biobank publication. After that I developed the sleep detection algorithms on other datasets which have by now also been applied to UK Biobank.

The IV IS variables in GGIR are among the few variables I implemented without a thorough evaluation, because to evaluate them you would have to compare them with conventional actigraphy methods or look at consistency in associations with health and demographic information.

A good starting point to start the implementation is the documentation for the function g.IVIS in https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/GGIR/GGIR.pdf. The function arguments you see there can also be supplied to g.shell.GGIR (explained in the vignette). So, you do not need to interact with the g.IVIS function directly.

Argument IVIS.activity.metric=1 (the current default) makes that it uses my first (naive) implementation of IVIS. However, after talking to van Someren I became aware that an alternative way of quantifying the magnitude of movement inside the IVIS calculation would be more meaningful. I implemented that and you can use this implementation via IVIS.activity.metric=2. So, if you specify the results should become more plausible.

However, please check these variables critically, e.g. are the associations with health and demographic information as you expect?

If yes, then maybe this is a good time to make IVIS.activity.metric=2 the default. If not, then it would be good to do more research on this. For this it would be welcome if someone could finding funding for my time to be involved in the development/implementation of better algorithms.

The actual code of g.IVIS you can find here: https://github.com/wadpac/GGIR/blob/master/R/g.IVIS.R (I am aware that this may need to be tidied up a bit. I use the term Xi to make it consistent with the algorithm terminology used by van Someren).

I hope the above clarifies your questions, if not then let know.

Good point about adding more documentation about IVIS to the vignette. I will add it to the to do list.

Thanks,

Vincent

Dr. Vincent van Hees
Independent consultant

You can ignore "could not extract version", this relates to printing a context summary to the the console. It plays no role in the analysis and will be fixed in the next CRAN release, and it is already fixed in the GGIR beta-version 2.2-1 on GitHub.

The other issue may indicate:
- File is open, if yes, close it.
- File has no data. I see this is Actigraph, use Actilife to check whether there is data
- File is not a raw data file. Raw data files in csv format should be at least several 100 MB in size.
- The file is somehow not readable.

Also I gave you hints at what you could do in our other conversation, did you follow those?

Thanks,
Vincent

messages.subject: Re: [GGIR] code for identifying work days and non work days
messages.subject_clean: [GGIR] code for identifying work days and non work days
messages.body_plain:
In the person level output GGIR splits the week in weekend- and in weekdays. If you prefer to aggregate data in a different way, e.g. based on a diary of when people worked or based on a different definition of "weekend", then I would advise to use the day summary output and aggregate it yourself. Just add a column of when people worked and then most statistical packages should offer some kind of aggregation option.
Best,
Vincent

See https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/GGIR/vignettes/GGIR.html#waking-waking-or-24-hour-time-use-analysis
These are the timewindows defined in part 5, either based on midnight-midnight days or based on wakingup-wakingup (WW) windows. I called it window number instead of day number to emphasize that these are time windows that typically overlap with two calendar days.

messages.subject: Re: [GGIR] IV/IS specifications
messages.body_plain:
... now see I forgot to respond to your 2nd question "Additionally, I was wondering how the setting of these parameters interferes with the ws2 epoch size specification. "

All parts of GGIR, including IVIS, account for epoch sizes chosen in GGIR part 1. However, the resulting algorithm may of course change when working with different epoch sizes. The IVIS calculation uses a rolling sum (when using the metric 2 I mentioned) and a rolling average of 10 minutes or longer. See also the code link I shared in my previous message. So, I would not expect that choosing 5, 30 or 60 second epoch makes a big difference. But it is probably good to double check in your own data.

Thanks,
Vincent

messages.subject: Re: [GGIR] Only getting 6 days of data in part 5 instead of 7 (missing the final day)
messages.subject_clean: [GGIR] Only getting 6 days of data in part 5 instead of 7 (missing the final day)
messages.body_plain:
Hi Aiden,

This is expected behavior from GGIR. GGIR only estimates sleep for 'nights' where there is at least a midnight timestamp in the data. The last midnight in your data is missing, by which GGIR assumes that sleep onset time cannot be reliably estimated. This in turn makes using the last measurement day questionable because we do not know when it's waking hours ended.

We could adapt or trick the algorithm to include the last day, but I am not sure that is a good idea. However, if you have good reasons to expect that most of your participants fall a sleep long before 23:45 then it seems justifiable to try to develop a work around.

This requires additional development work on GGIR, which I am afraid I can only do as a part of a paid consultancy. Let me know if you want to discuss this.

Best wishes,

Vincent

Dr. Vincent van Hees

Subject: Re: [GGIR] IV/IS specifications

Dear Renske,

Thanks for researching out.

On side note - About GGIR and UK Biobank, it is more the other way around. UK Biobank gained a lot from the work I did around GGIR. I developed most of GGIR between 2008-2013 using the Whitehall II study and the Pelotas birth cohorts as primary testing ground. My PhD in those years was focussed on guide UK Biobank in deciding whether to use wrist worn accelerometer and how to analyse it. The 2011 PLoSONE study I led on was one of the key reasons for UK Biobank to go ahead with using wrist accelerometry. The algorithms I developed in those years where then later copied to Java software by Doherty and colleagues in their 2017 UK Biobank publication. After that I developed the sleep detection algorithms on other datasets which have by now also been applied to UK Biobank.

The IV IS variables in GGIR are among the few variables I implemented without a thorough evaluation, because to evaluate them you would have to compare them with conventional actigraphy methods or look at consistency in associations with health and demographic information.

A good starting point to start the implementation is the documentation for the function g.IVIS in https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/GGIR/GGIR.pdf. The function arguments you see there can also be supplied to g.shell.GGIR (explained in the vignette). So, you do not need to interact with the g.IVIS function directly.

Argument IVIS.activity.metric=1 (the current default) makes that it uses my first (naive) implementation of IVIS. However, after talking to van Someren I became aware that an alternative way of quantifying the magnitude of movement inside the IVIS calculation would be more meaningful. I implemented that and you can use this implementation via IVIS.activity.metric=2. So, if you specify the results should become more plausible.

However, please check these variables critically, e.g. are the associations with health and demographic information as you expect?

If yes, then maybe this is a good time to make IVIS.activity.metric=2 the default. If not, then it would be good to do more research on this. For this it would be welcome if someone could finding funding for my time to be involved in the development/implementation of better algorithms.

The actual code of g.IVIS you can find here: https://github.com/wadpac/GGIR/blob/master/R/g.IVIS.R (I am aware that this may need to be tidied up a bit. I use the term Xi to make it consistent with the algorithm terminology used by van Someren).

I hope the above clarifies your questions, if not then let know.

Good point about adding more documentation about IVIS to the vignette. I will add it to the to do list.

Thanks,

Vincent

Dr. Vincent van Hees

There have been a couple of conversations in this google group around this topic in recent months, e.g. questions from Dora. So, maybe it is easiest if you could checkout those conversations first and see whether you could exchange experiences with her or others.

For me it really helps if people could post a detailed and reproducible example of the issue they are running into, so including sessionInfo() output, R scripts/commands used, and milestone data file.

Calendar date is the date on which the WW window starts.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Vincent,

We processed the files using GGIR version 2.2-0. Then, we have reprocessed only part2 to include another mvpa threshold to be reported in part2_daysummary_longformat.
We have checked the discussion on Dora's topic. You presented an example of a situation when this issue may occur in WW output. But in our case, the onset was after midnight in both entries, so we expected to see different calendar dates.

The metafiles of these two participants are attached to help you with reproducible examples. We also attached the script and sessioninfo() output as .txt files.

Our intention is to model the effect of time-specific PA estimates from p2 on the following night's sleep. So, we need to match part2 daily estimates with part5_WW. The part5_MM sleep estimates are expected to not compute data from the same night and may be inadequate to use. Is this correct?

Thank you for your support,

Marcus Lopes and colleagues.
